The launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 is set to become a huge online event as YouTube has announced a special 24-hour global livestream featuring more than 30 gaming creators and internet personalities. The broadcast will begin on November 19, with a special pre-show hosted by RDCWorld on the night before. The event will include live gameplay, creator podcasts and other special content. It will also feature popular Indian gaming creators Payal Gaming and Total Gaming, giving Indian fans more reasons to tune in.YouTube has announced that its GTA 6 launch livestream will run for 24 hours, bringing together creators from different parts of the world. The main livestream will then start at midnight ET on November 19, the same time GTA 6 officially launches in the US.YouTube has described the event with the tagline,According to YouTube's official blog, the broadcast will feature live gameplay, creator podcasts and original content.The event will also end with special coverage from Miami, where creators and guests will come together.One of the biggest highlights of the YouTube GTA 6 livestream is its list of more than 30 creators. The lineup includes gaming personalities from several countries, making it a global celebration of the game's launch.Indian fans will be able to watch some familiar faces during the event. Payal Gaming, Total Gaming and Sharkshe are among the Indian creators included in the announced lineup.Other popular gaming creators include Caylus, Jelly, Zhong, Nought, Cinna, Loserfruit, TGG and JoblessGarrett. Indian viewers can also join the event from the morning of November 19 and watch their favourite creators take part in the launch festivities.
Article Summary: YouTube announces 24-hour GTA 6 global livestream with 30+ creators. The broadcast will begin on November 19, with a special pre-show hosted by RDCWorld on the night before. The event will include live gameplay, creator podcasts and other special content.

Article Title: A Washington boy who was autistic, nonverbal and legally blind died at 15 after years of abuse in his adoptive home; six years later, his estate and brothers secured a $49.33 million settlement
Article Text:
Karreon Adams-Franks Photo: Fox12

What happened to Karreon

The warnings the state received

What schools knew

The settlement and who pays

What the district said

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Why the case matters

Karreon Adams-Franks was 15 years old, autistic, nonverbal, and legally blind when he died in his Vancouver, Washington, home in 2020 after years of abuse and starvation. Six years later, his estate and his two surviving brothers have secured a $49.33 million settlement from the State of Washington and Evergreen Public Schools, according to reporting by Oregon Public Broadcasting, KPTV, and the Davis Law Group.The settlement resolves claims that state child welfare agencies and the school district failed to act on repeated warnings before Karreon’s death. His adoptive parents were convicted in 2023 of homicide by abuse and criminal mistreatment, but the civil case focused on whether the institutions responsible for protecting children also failed him.Karreon was adopted by his biological aunt, Felicia Adams, and her partner, Jesse Franks. He and his two younger brothers lived in their Vancouver home, where attorneys said the boys endured years of abuse, including beatings, choking, confinement, and food being withheld as punishment.Karreon was completely dependent on the adults around him for daily care. At the time of his death on November 27, 2020, he weighed 61 pounds.In 2023, Adams and Franks were convicted of homicide by abuse in Karreon’s death and criminal mistreatment of his brothers.Adams was sentenced to 35 years in prison, while Franks received 30 years. The Washington Court of Appeals upheld both convictions and sentences in March 2026.The lawsuit alleged that the Washington Department of Children, Youth and Families and the Department of Social and Health Services received reports about the family as early as 2017. Two referrals that year alleged that food was being withheld from the children as punishment.On November 20, 2020, a relative told the state that Karreon looked like a walking skeleton and was falling down because of malnourishment. A social worker visited the home the next day and described him as very skinny, but the lawsuit said the worker did not arrange medical care or remove the boys from the home.Karreon died six days later. The family’s attorneys argued that the state’s failure to investigate properly and act on the warnings contributed to the harm the boys suffered.Karreon and his brothers attended Evergreen Public Schools, including Shahala Middle School and Mountain View High School. The lawsuit alleged that staff documented concerns about the boys for years but did not report suspected abuse to law enforcement or the state.In May 2018, one of the boys told a school bus driver that food had been withheld from him over an entire weekend. According to the lawsuit, the concern was relayed back to Felicia Adams, the person accused of abusing him, and the boy was beaten in retaliation.School records obtained by KPTV included an educator’s note saying that the parents withheld food as a form of discipline. Another note described Karreon eating breakfast and refusing to leave the table until he received more food.The settlement was reached on October 8, 2026, days before a trial was scheduled to begin in Clark County Superior Court. It resolves claims brought by Karreon’s estate and his two surviving brothers.The State of Washington agreed to pay $25 million, while Evergreen Public Schools is paying $24.3 million. The school district’s payment represents the full amount of insurance coverage available to it, according to the Davis Law Group.Evergreen said the decision to settle was made by its insurers to avoid the risk of a jury verdict exceeding the district’s available coverage. The district said it maintained that none of its staff failed to make a mandatory report to the state or law enforcement.In a statement, Evergreen Public Schools said it recognises the profound loss of Karreon’s life and the lasting impact on his family. The district described the situation as tragic and said the perpetrators of the crimes are in prison.The district also said it hopes the settlement will allow Karreon’s brothers to continue healing without having to endure a trial. It said the staff who worked with the three boys were caring and dedicated educators who had the boys’ best interests at heart.The school district’s statement did not dispute the settlement itself, but it pushed back on the claim that staff failed to meet their reporting obligations. The distinction matters because the civil case was about institutional responsibility, not just the actions of the adoptive parents.The settlement highlights the role that schools and child welfare agencies can play in identifying abuse before it becomes fatal. Under Washington law, school employees who have reasonable cause to believe a child is being abused or neglected must report it to law enforcement or the state.Attorney Chris Davis said, as per the reports, that no amount of money can make up for what happened to Karreon and what his brothers endured. He said the people and agencies responsible for protecting them saw warning signs for years and did not act.For Karreon’s brothers, the settlement may provide financial stability and support for recovery. For the wider community, it serves as a reminder that every warning sign deserves serious attention, because a child’s life may depend on it.
Article Summary: Karreon Adams-Franks was 15 years old, autistic, nonverbal, and legally blind when he died in his Vancouver, Washington, home in 2020 after years of abuse and starvation. His adoptive parents were convicted in 2023 of homicide by abuse and criminal mistreatment, but the civil case focused on whether the institutions responsible for protecting children also failed him. The settlement resolves claims that state child welfare agencies and the school district failed to act on repeated warnings before Karreon’s death.

Article Title: 'I have never stolen': Mongolia's president announces resignation over $25 million bribery allegations
Article Text:
File photo: Mongolia's President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa speaks during a news conference where he announced he would resign

Railway contract at centre of bribery allegations

Parliament must approve resignation

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa on Tuesday announced that he would step down following allegations that he received a $25 million bribe linked to a government railway contract awarded in 2019, when he was prime minister.Khurelsukh has denied wrongdoing but said he would cooperate with investigators and relinquish office so the allegations against him could be examined.“I have never stolen from my people or my state,” he said in a televised address to the nation. “I will hand over my duties as president and become an ordinary citizen.”The allegations were made by Nyambaatar Khishgee, the former mayor of the capital Ulaanbaatar and a member of the ruling Mongolian People's Party (MPP), but from a different faction within the party. He accused Khurelsukh of receiving $25 million in connection with the Tavantolgoi-Gashuunsukhait railway project.The opposition Democratic Party subsequently demanded the president's resignation, saying the allegations reflected corruption and cronyism among leaders of the ruling party.The accusations concern the awarding of a railway contract in 2019 to Bodi International LLC, one of Mongolia's largest conglomerates.Khurelsukh, who was prime minister at the time, is alleged to have ensured that the contract went to the company without a competitive bidding process and received money in return.Bodi International denied the allegations on Monday, saying it had not paid cash bribes to senior government officials or civil servants. The company described the accusations as defamatory and maintained that it had done nothing wrong.Two other senior officials named in the allegations also announced their resignations on Tuesday. They were Deputy Minister of Justice and Home Affairs Munkh-Erdene Dembereltseren and Cabinet Secretariat head Enkhbayar Battumur.Khurelsukh said he had faced sustained attacks on his reputation for more than a month. In his address, he said he agreed with the Democratic Party's demand that he step aside so the allegations could be investigated.“I will be investigated and will have my honour restored,” he said, according to the state-run Montsame news agency.Khurelsukh's announcement does not immediately remove him from office. Under Mongolian law, a presidential resignation must be approved by the 126-member State Great Khural, the country's unicameral parliament.The legislature is expected to meet later this week to consider his resignation. If it accepts the decision, the parliamentary speaker will serve as interim president.The resignation announcement comes amid divisions within the ruling MPP, which has been hit by internal power struggles in recent years. Mongolia has seen three prime ministers take office in just nine months, highlighting the instability within the governing party.Khurelsukh had also resigned as prime minister in January 2021 to contest the presidential election. He won the presidency six months later, while the MPP secured a majority in parliament.The current allegations have therefore opened a fresh political test for the ruling party and its leadership, with the president's future now dependent on parliament's decision and the outcome of the investigation.
Article Summary: Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa announced that he would step down following allegations that he received a $25 million bribe linked to a government railway contract awarded in 2019. The allegations were made by Nyambaatar Khishgee, the former mayor of the capital Ulaanbaatar and a member of the ruling Mongolian People's Party (MPP) Two other senior officials also announced their resignations on Tuesday.

Article Title: A 14-year-old US student collects used coffee grounds from nearly a dozen cafes to grow oyster mushrooms; through her nonprofit, Fungi For Future, she hopes to reduce food waste and help tackle hunger
Article Text:
PC: WFIU & WTIU News/Youtube

How is Gloria Chi collecting coffee grounds to grow mushrooms

From a science project to mushroom-growing buckets

How oyster mushrooms turn coffee grounds into nutrient-rich compost

What does Gloria Chi hope to achieve through ‘Fungi For Future’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A 14-year-old eighth-grader in Bloomington, Indiana, is collecting coffee grounds from nearly a dozen local coffee shops and turning them into material for growing oyster mushrooms. Gloria Chi started her nonprofit, ‘Fungi For Future’, in March, after starting the project. The initiative gives discarded coffee grounds a second life by turning them into a growing medium for mushrooms.Chi has repurposed more than 122 pounds of coffee grounds in her family’s basement, where mushrooms grow in plastic buckets filled with layers of grounds and straw. According to Indiana Public Media, the project has expanded beyond food production to reducing food waste and helping the environment. She plans to donate harvested mushrooms to Hoosier Hills Food Bank and give the remaining mixture to local orchards and composters.Chi attends Jackson Creek Middle School and has been collecting coffee grounds from nearly a dozen coffee shops in Bloomington. Her partners include Starbucks, Soma Coffee House & Juice Bar, Crumble Coffee and Bakery, The Inkwell Bakery & Cafe, Hopscotch Coffee and the Bloomington Bagel Company.At Crumble Coffee and Bakery, baristas collect the used grounds in a three-gallon bucket behind the counter on Saturdays instead of throwing them away. Chi collects the bucket before the shop closes. The shop uses at least one five-pound bag of espresso beans daily, and often more during Indiana University semesters. Chi began the project in early March and said collecting the grounds has not always gone smoothly.Chi moved to Bloomington from Pennsylvania in July 2025. Before turning to mushrooms, she tried growing tropical fruit trees, but said the cold weather made the project difficult. She said, “It was, like, really hard because, like, it was cold, and for tropical fruit trees, you need to be warm.”“It was sort of like a failed project.”By September, she had shifted her attention to fungi after researching mushroom cultivation online. She first used a mushroom-growing kit to learn the basics. When those mushrooms died, she decided to try growing them herself.Chi ordered mushroom spawn online and began filling buckets with layers of coffee grounds and straw. In her family’s basement, she has 10 five-gallon buckets with holes drilled into their sides. Pink, blue and pearl oyster mushrooms grow through the openings, while white mycelium spreads through the mixture inside.Oyster mushrooms survive by breaking down and digesting dead organic matter. As mycelium spreads through the buckets, it breaks down complex compounds in the coffee grounds. Indiana University biology professor Richard Phillips said, “Fungi produce extracellular enzymes.”“These are enzymes that release out into the soil and are involved in decomposition.”As the grounds decompose, nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium become more available for plants to absorb. The leftover mixture of coffee grounds, straw, and mycelium can then be used as compost. Chi plans to donate it to local orchards and composters after harvesting the mushrooms.She referred to mycoremediation, a process she described as mushrooms cleansing toxic material, and said the mixture should make good fertiliser.Chi hoped her mushrooms could become a sustainable food source.She said, “I'm not growing as many mushrooms as I thought I would.”“I was really hoping I could solve hunger with my mushrooms.”The project has also taken on a wider purpose that is reducing food waste and helping the environment. Phillips said similar projects could potentially grow beyond one basement operation if more people became involved.Phillips said, “It sounds like the kind of project that could probably scale up very well, if it's something that a lot of people got interested and involved in.”“That could definitely have an impact on reducing food waste.”Chi has received $1,500 in grants and continues to apply for further financial support. She is working with food resource organisations around Bloomington. She said, “I am looking into some help from the community.”“I hope I can do this forever but I can’t do all this work by myself.”
Article Summary: Gloria Chi started her nonprofit, ‘Fungi For Future’, in March, after starting the project. The initiative gives discarded coffee grounds a second life by turning them into a growing medium for mushrooms. Chi has repurposed more than 122 pounds of coffee grounds.

Article Title: Mexico, China push cooperation despite tariff tensions ahead of APEC
Article Text:
File photo: Delegations led by Chinese President Xi Jinping, right, and Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum, left, attend a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC)

Mexico looks to China for waste-to-energy technology

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

First China visit as president

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on Tuesday told Chinese President Xi Jinping that Mexico wanted to expand cooperation with Beijing, as the two leaders met in Shenzhen ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.The meeting comes as trade tensions between the two countries grew, especially after Mexico approved tariffs of up to 50% on more than 1,400 products imported from China and other countries that do not have free trade agreements with Mexico. The duties, which took effect in January, cover sectors including automobiles, auto parts, textiles, footwear and household appliances.China has criticised the measures, while Mexico has defended them as necessary to protect domestic manufacturing. Despite the dispute, Beijing remains a major economic partner for Mexico, accounting for its second-largest source of imports after the United States. Bilateral trade has exceeded $100 billion annually since 2023.One of the areas where Mexico is seeking Chinese expertise is waste management, particularly technology that can convert discarded material into energy while reducing dependence on landfills.Mexico is considering a shift towards a waste-to-energy model as part of its efforts to build a circular economy.The approach could help generate cleaner energy, address waste disposal challenges and free up land currently used for dumping.Ahead of the summit, Mexican environment minister Alicia Bárcena visited Chinese facilities specialising in waste utilisation and water treatment to assess whether their technologies could be adapted for use in Mexico.Mexico's environment ministry said the visit was intended to identify alternatives for improving the country's waste management system.Bárcena also visited the Honghu underground wastewater treatment plant in Shenzhen, which can process up to 100,000 tonnes of wastewater a day.The facility has a public park above ground, with the minister making note and stating that Shenzhen offered an example of how polluted waterways and degraded ecosystems could be restored while creating areas for community use.“The Chinese experience demonstrates that it is possible to move beyond landfills and advance toward a circular economy model,” Bárcena said.Sheinbaum arrived in Shenzhen on Monday for her first visit to China as president. Her bilateral meeting with Xi had been confirmed by the Mexican presidency ahead of the November 18-19 APEC summit.The Mexican leader is also expected to promote her government's Plan Mexico investment strategy during the visit. Her schedule includes meetings with leaders from Canada, Australia and Vietnam.The Shenzhen summit is expected to bring together several major regional and global leaders, including US President Donald Trump and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
Article Summary: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum told Chinese President Xi Jinping that Mexico wanted to expand cooperation with Beijing. The two leaders met in Shenzhen ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. Mexico is seeking Chinese expertise in waste management, particularly technology that can convert discarded material into energy while reducing dependence on landfills.

Article Title: West Virginia's state auditor has been indicted after prosecutors alleged he overrode staff objections to issue tax deeds for nine properties to benefit a friend, allegedly taking land from its rightf
Article Text:
West Virginia Auditor Mark Hunt.

Why the nine property transfers are under investigation

Separate bank fraud allegations involve state employee

Two officials face additional charges over FBI interviews

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

West Virginia State Auditor Mark A. Hunt has been indicted by a federal grand jury over allegations that he used his office to help a longtime friend and business associate obtain nine tax-delinquent properties, overriding objections from staff who said the transfers were not legally permitted.Hunt, 66, is among four men charged with nine counts of theft of property in connection with the alleged scheme. The indictment also names two senior officials from the auditor's office and a state employee in separate allegations involving falsified government timecards and bank fraud.US Attorney Moore Capito announced the charges, saying the investigation concerned the alleged misuse of public office for personal benefit.The properties are located in Kanawha and Boone counties and were being sought by a business entity associated with Robert Lisle Johns, 66, described by prosecutors as Hunt's longtime friend and business associate.Employees in the auditor's Land Division determined that all nine properties were ineligible for deed issuance because the purchaser had failed to make the required payments and submit paperwork within statutory deadlines, according to the indictment.Prosecutors allege Hunt proceeded despite these objections. He personally signed deeds for eight properties on March 28 last year followed by the ninth on June 6. Hunt had taken office in January that year.The indictment alleges that Hunt was assisted by David Keith Cole, the deputy chief of staff in the auditor's office, and Frederic Scott Caudill, its general counsel. Johns was appointed special counsel to the office in June 2025.Prosecutors allege the four men were involved in the issuance of the deeds, resulting in the properties being taken from their lawful owners.The grand jury also indicted Hunt and Cole alongside Marie Ann Hoffmann, 66, an employee of the state auditor's office, in a separate bank fraud case.According to prosecutors, Hoffmann submitted falsified government timecards that included hours she had spent working at Hunt's private law firm, Mark A. Hunt & Associates. The alleged arrangement ran from May 5, to at least September 29 this year.Hoffmann was a full-time state employee who left her government duty station on Friday afternoons to perform paralegal and administrative work at the private firm. Hunt and Cole also frequently worked with her there during state business hours, according to the indictment.Cole approved the falsified timecards, enabling Hoffmann to receive wages from the West Virginia Treasury for work she had not performed for the state auditor's office. Hunt was aware of the arrangement, according to prosecutors.Cole and Caudill have each been charged with making materially false statements to federal investigators during interviews concerning the disputed property deeds.Caudill allegedly made false statements during an FBI interview on October 26 including about whether he had asked staff who would act as a whistleblower over the handling of the deeds.Cole is accused of making false statements during an October 6 interview about the property transfers and his approval of Hoffmann's timecards.The theft charges carry a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000. Making materially false statements to federal investigators carries a maximum five-year prison term, while bank fraud carries up to 30 years in prison and a fine of up to $1 million.West Virginia State Treasurer Larry Pack called for Hunt's resignation following the indictment, saying the allegations required serious attention and that residents deserved transparency and accountability from elected officials.
Article Summary: West Virginia State Auditor Mark A. Hunt has been indicted by a federal grand jury over allegations that he used his office to help a longtime friend and business associate obtain nine tax-delinquent properties. Hunt, 66, is among four men charged with nine counts of theft of property in connection with the alleged scheme.

A massive fire ripped through a commercial building on Thailand's southern resort island of Phuket early on Monday, killing at least 11 people and leaving 16 others injured, police told Reuters. The blaze broke out in the early hours of the morning and quickly spread to several nearby buildings, triggering a major firefighting operation.The fire erupted at around 3.17am local time (2017 GMT) at a shophouse housing a vehicle rental business. Firefighters battled the flames for nearly two hours before bringing the blaze under control, Thai authorities said.Of the 16 injured, 15 were Thai nationals while one was from Myanmar, police said. No tourists were among those killed or injured in the incident.The building is located in a town area near Patong, one of Phuket's most popular beach destinations on the island's western coast. The incident raised concerns as the fire spread beyond the building where it first broke out, engulfing several neighbouring structures.The cause of the fire remains under investigation, with authorities yet to establish what triggered the blaze.The incident comes just four months after a deadly fire at a bar in Bangkok claimed at least 27 lives, highlighting another major fire tragedy in Thailand.Make the intro more directRemove repeated fire detailsUse a sharper news structure

Article Title: JD Vance says US will not fight 'forever war' with Iran, defends Donald Trump's military action
Article Text:
File photo: US President Donald Trump with Vice President JD Vance

Vance says there is ‘no daylight’ between him and Trump

Third US aircraft carrier arrives in Middle East

Trump to discuss Iran war at summit with Xi and Putin

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

US vice president JD Vance has said President Donald Trump will not allow the conflict with Iran to turn into a “forever war”, ruling out even a two-year American military commitment while defending the decision to target Tehran's nuclear programme.In an interview with Fox News host Laura Ingraham on Monday (local time), Vance said he was confident Trump would bring the conflict to an end, although he did not provide a specific timeline for ending US military involvement.“He is not going to let this become a forever war,” Vance said. “We told the American people we would do no more forever wars.”He added that the administration would not allow the conflict to become a “10- or 15-year commitment, or frankly, even a two-year commitment”, despite pressure from what he described as neoconservatives and others who wanted the US to remain involved indefinitely.Vance defended Trump's decision to target Iran's nuclear programme, describing it as a threat to the United States. He also said he had full confidence that the president would bring the conflict to a close with “great results”.The vice president also insisted that he and Trump were aligned on the Iran war, despite having publicly blamed the conflict for the Republican Party's poor performance in the midterm elections.“There’s no daylight, Laura,” Vance told Ingraham, adding that there was no disagreement between the president and other senior members of the administration.However, he acknowledged that the war had carried a political cost, pointing to higher petrol and energy prices. Vance also cited a lack of investment in American energy infrastructure over recent decades as another factor behind rising fuel costs.Earlier this month, following the Republican defeat in the midterms, Vance wrote on X, “The reason we lost is the war.”He had also challenged Republicans who believed the military campaign was worth the electoral cost, writing, “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.”Trump subsequently said he believed Vance's assessment was correct, but added that the vice president should also have said that he would support launching the operation again if given the choice.The comments came after Trump announced last week that Vance would no longer be involved in negotiations with Iran and would instead focus on alleged government benefits fraud.Vance also used the Fox News interview to defend the administration's economic approach, calling for a renewed focus on domestic manufacturing and bringing factories and jobs back to the US.He said the election results showed that Americans wanted prosperity, freedom and sovereignty, while acknowledging that many were facing economic difficulties.Vance's remarks came as the US increased its naval presence in the Middle East, with the USS Theodore Roosevelt arriving in the region on Monday.The US military said the aircraft carrier was operating in the area covered by US Central Command as part of a scheduled deployment. Its arrival brought the number of American carrier strike groups in the region to three, alongside the USS George HW Bush and the USS George Washington.The Roosevelt and its accompanying ships add to a US naval presence that includes more than a dozen destroyers,.The deployment comes amid continued tensions between Washington and Tehran. Iran said on Sunday that its forces had carried out a drone attack on a US radar system at a helicopter base in Bahrain. Bahrain's military said it intercepted the drones before they could reach their intended targets.Iran had launched drones towards Bahrain on Friday, marking the first such strikes against Gulf countries since September. US Central Command said it had shot down two Iranian drones on that occasion, with no casualties or damage reported.Efforts to end the conflict have made little progress. Tehran has demanded the release of frozen assets held abroad, sanctions relief and an end to the US naval blockade of Iranian ports in exchange for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.Iran has said it is ready to reopen the waterway within two days if Washington accepts its conditions.Trump is also expected to discuss the conflict at a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on Thursday.China's foreign ministry confirmed on Monday that Xi would host the meeting. Spokesperson Mao Ning described it as the first in-person meeting between the heads of state of the three countries, with discussions expected to focus on global peace and strategic stability.Mao did not confirm whether Iran or nuclear arms control would feature on the agenda, saying further details would be shared as preparations progressed.Beijing also announced that its special envoy for the Middle East, Zhai Jun, had recently visited Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia for diplomatic consultations aimed at easing regional tensions.Trump has said he intends to raise the Iran conflict during the summit, even as he has maintained that a formal peace deal with Tehran is not necessary to bring the fighting to an end.
Article Summary: Third US aircraft carrier arrives in Middle East.Trump to discuss Iran war at summit with Xi and Putin. US vice president JD Vance says there is 'no daylight' between him and Trump. US increased its naval presence in the region on Monday.

Fire outside Met stadium

A fire broke out in an empty postgame tent outside MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Sunday, sending thick clouds of smoke billowing over the venue hours after the New York Jets suffered their fifth consecutive defeat of the NFL season.Videos shared on social media showed large plumes of smoke rising near the stadium in East Rutherford and drifting over the playing field. One video also captured flames and black smoke erupting from the area near the venue.New Jersey State Police said troopers responded to a report of smoke shortly after 5:50 pm near Lot A and the stadium's American Express gate. They found a fire in an empty postgame tent, according to a report by Fox 5 New York.Fire crews brought the second-alarm blaze under control. No injuries or further damage were reported, while the cause of the fire was not immediately known.ESPN reporter Rich Cimini posted on social media that an announcement had been made inside the stadium about a “structure fire” near the adjacent train station. He later advised people to stay away from the stadium's east plaza, on the train station side, as smoke spread across the venue.Around 20 minutes later, he posted that the “situation has been resolved”.An NJ Transit spokesperson, quoted by NY Post said the fire did not disrupt train services in the area.The blaze broke out hours after the Jets lost 31-12 to the Buffalo Bills at MetLife Stadium. The defeat marked their fifth straight loss, leaving them with a 2-8 record for the season.The Jets struggled against the Bills, who secured a 19-point victory. The loss extended New York's losing streak and added to a difficult season for the team.
Article Summary: Fire broke out in an empty postgame tent outside MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Sunday. The blaze sent thick clouds of smoke billowing over the venue hours after the New York Jets suffered their fifth consecutive defeat of the NFL season. No injuries or further damage were reported. The cause of the fire was not immediately known.

The sons of imprisoned former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan have accused authorities of subjecting their father to prolonged physical and mental torture in Adiala Jail, warning that he could die in custody without urgent medical intervention.In an interview with Sky News's Mark Austin, Sulaiman Isa Khan and Kasim Khan expressed concern over the deteriorating health of the 74-year-old Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder, alleging that he was being kept in solitary confinement for 22 to 23 hours a day, with little human contact and no access to independent medical care."We can see the path that this is taking. It's inevitable that eventually he will die in this cell. He will be killed in this cell if he remains there any longer without proper treatment," the brothers said.They also alleged that prison authorities had instructed guards not to speak to their father, adding that the isolation was being used to exert psychological pressure on him."I mean, we've been saying this for months. They're torturing him in the cell. It's physical and mental torture. It's at a point where they've instructed the guards not to even speak to him while he's in the cell just to, you know, maintain pressure and mental pressure on him," they added.The brothers said authorities had failed to implement an August 18 Supreme Court order directing that Khan be shifted to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad for medical examination and treatment. The order had also called for increased family access, including regular telephone conversations with his sons."Nothing's changed at all, despite an order from the Supreme Court back in August for him to be taken and treated at a private hospital called Shifa International, and for increased family access to his family, calls with us, regular calls with us. But none of that has been implemented. And his health has just continued to deteriorate," they said."His blood pressure is now dangerously high, at about 193, I think. So he needs to be treated at a private hospital immediately," they added.The interview comes as Khan has appealed to Pakistan's top judges through an open letter, seeking urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife, Bushra Bibi. He said his blood pressure had risen sharply and doctors had warned of the risk of a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest.In the letter, released by his party and lawyer Salman Safdar, Khan also alleged that authorities had failed to implement the earlier hospital transfer order. "I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive," he said.However, Pakistan's cabinet minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry disputed Khan's claims, saying he had received regular medical attention and had been taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad eight times for examinations. The government has also rejected allegations of solitary confinement and denied that Khan was being denied access to his family.
Article Summary: Sulaiman Isa Khan and Kasim Khan accuse authorities of subjecting their father to prolonged physical and mental torture in Adiala Jail. They allege that he is being kept in solitary confinement for 22 to 23 hours a day, with little human contact and no access to independent medical care. Khan has appealed to Pakistan's top judges, seeking urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife.

Article Title: Scientists tracked Manx shearwaters across the Atlantic for two decades and found that fast eastward flights can give birds jet lag; even experienced adults drift off course before correcting their ro
Article Text:
Manx Shearwaters, the marine birds that hunt over the open ocean Image credits: Oxford University

How a slow body clock sends birds the wrong way

Infographic showing clock-shift that occurs during homing flights of shearwaters. The bird begins to home at point A. On the first day of homing, its endogenous clock is calibrated to local time at 30°W. However, the shearwater travels eastwards to 15°W over 6 hours to point B. Here, sunrise happened an hour earlier, so the shearwater’s perceived time lags local time by an hour and the sun is roughly 20° further clockwise than the shearwater expects. At point B, this discrepancy causes the shearwater to orient roughly 20° clockwise of the correct direction. Image Credits: Credit: Lewin et al, 2026. Oxford University

Small errors for adults, bigger risks for first-timers

Manx shearwater in flight over sea Image credits: thelonekayaker/ wordpress

Manx Shearwater Puffinus puffinus Image credits: birdsoftheworld.org

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Manx shearwaters flying home from feeding trips can be nudged off course by a kind of jet lag, researchers say. It happens when a bird’s body clock falls out of step with the local time. Tracking data from Manx shearwaters on the west coast of the UK revealed that when the birds returned home to their colonies after trips over the Atlantic, their rapid eastward flights disrupted their sense of time and navigation.When humans get jet lag, we fly across time zones and feel tired and out of sync because our body clock is still running on the old time. Shearwaters seem to have a similar problem. For them, it shows up as a wrong turn over the open sea.A studyfinds that long-distance flights can throw seabirds' internal clocks out of sync, causing navigation errors , it was published in October 2026 on the Oxford University website. It talks about how researchers in Oxford University's Department of Biology analysed 20 years of GPS tracking data from 1,045 breeding shearwaters, covering 3,688 foraging trips. The birds set off from colonies on the west coasts of the UK and Ireland. Some flew about 1,000km west to find food. On the way home, they flew east, back to their nests.Like many animals, shearwaters use the sun as a compass. This is very useful over open water, where there are no roads or landmarks. But the sun moves across the sky during the day, so a bird needs to know the time to work out where the sun should be. The bird’s body clock gives it that information. It is called the circadian rhythm. Birds normally reset their clocks at sunrise. That works well while a bird stays in one place. But when a bird travels quickly east or west, its clock can fall out of sync with local solar time. On the flight home, the shearwaters crossed places where the sun rises earlier. The Oxford release says this can leave their clocks lagging behind local time by up to around one hour.The researchers worked out how a slow clock should change the birds’ sun compass. Then they compared those predictions with the directions the GPS trackers recorded. As the birds travelled east, they tended to drift clockwise from their expected direction. That is what you would expect if their clocks were running behind. The team from the Department of Biology found that when the predicted compass error pointed towards land, the shearwaters flew closer to the coast. When it pointed away from land, they flew further out to sea. So the birds seem to use the sun compass even when familiar land is close by.The errors were real, but they were small. In “Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course,” published by Science News on October 29, 2026, Anirban Mukhopadhyay reports that the birds veered by as much as 15 degrees. The errors were small enough to add only a few kilometres to the journey. They were not enough to stop the shearwaters from finding their way home.Adult birds can fix their mistakes because they keep checking where they are. The Oxford team calculated that a shearwater returning from 1,000 km away with an average compass error of seven degrees would fly only about 5 km further than needed to get within 5 km of its colony.“It’s inherently difficult to study the cognitive processes of animals in the wild, so it’s exciting to realise that if we measure their natural movements carefully enough we can reveal the underlying behavioural mechanisms.” - Co-author Professor Tim Guilford, Department of Biology, Oxford University. The consequences could be more significant for animals that cannot continuously reassess and correct their positions.For example, young birds undertaking their first migration could be particularly vulnerable. Small navigational errors might accumulate over a long journey, potentially shifting their eventual destination by hundreds of kilometres.Researchers do not yet know whether the clock mismatch affects the birds in other ways. Internal clocks control many parts of an animal’s behaviour and body, so the problem could reach beyond navigation. More work is needed to find out. Dr Patrick Lewin, the lead researcher, has said that studying animals that regularly travel long distances could one day help us understand how humans cope with jet lag. “It’s amazing to think that billions of migratory animals look up to the sun for direction, relying on clocks silently ticking away inside them, and that errors in those clocks can cause them to take tiny shifts off course. ” - Lead researcher Dr Patrick Lewin, Department of Biology, Oxford University.
Article Summary: Manx shearwaters flying home from feeding trips can be nudged off course by a kind of jet lag, researchers say. It happens when a bird’s body clock falls out of step with the local time. For them, it shows up as a wrong turn over the open sea.

Article Title: From Russia-Ukraine war to Iran-US conflict: The return of the 'dirty bomb' threat
Article Text:
Representative image

What is a dirty bomb and how does it work?

How dangerous can a dirty bomb be?

Why are US officials concerned about the alleged Iranian plans?

What happens if a dirty bomb is detonated?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

US intelligence agencies have detected what officials describe as Iranian planning to potentially target senior members of President Donald Trump's administration in Washington DC using a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon, according to a CNN report citing seven US officials.The intelligence has triggered contingency planning in the United States, although officials remain divided over whether Iran has the capability or intention to carry out such an attack. Sources familiar with the assessment said the planning appeared to be an effort by Tehran to keep its options open rather than evidence of an imminent operationTwo sources cited by CNN claimed that the alleged plotting included specific locations and potential targets. US officials have also held several meetings over the past week to discuss ways to counter the threat.However, Iran's foreign ministry denied the report and termed the allegations as 'baseless'.White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said the administration was monitoring potential threats but added that “at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland”.The Iranian Mission to the United Nations in New York rejected allegations concerning chemical weapons, saying Iran “considers the use of chemical weapons under any circumstances to be wholly illegitimate and categorically rejects and unequivocally refutes the false and fabricated allegations circulated in this regard”.The statement did not explicitly address the intelligence about a possible dirty bomb plan.The reported threat comes as the US and Iran remain locked in conflict, with Washington continuing military strikes and an economic blockade against Tehran. Diplomatic efforts to end the hostilities have made little progress.Against this backdrop, the alleged planning has renewed attention on dirty bombs, which are different from nuclear weapons but can spread radioactive material over populated areas.A dirty bomb, technically known as a radiological dispersion device, combines conventional explosives with radioactive material. When the explosive detonates, it scatters the radioactive substance into the surrounding environment through dust, smoke and debris.Unlike a nuclear bomb, a dirty bomb does not trigger a nuclear-fission reaction. It does not produce a nuclear explosion capable of destroying an entire city. Instead, its purpose is to disperse radioactive contamination, potentially forcing people to evacuate affected areas and disrupting normal life.The device is considered relatively crude and easier to assemble than a nuclear weapon. It does not necessarily require sophisticated technology, although obtaining radioactive material remains a key challenge.Radioactive substances used in medicine, industrial equipment and research facilities could potentially be used in such a device.The quantity and type of radioactive material, the strength of the conventional explosive and weather conditions, particularly wind direction, would determine how widely contamination spreads.In 2022, the term “dirty bomb” became a talking point during the Russia-Ukraine war after Moscow accused Kyiv of preparing to use such a device on its own territory.Ukraine rejected the allegation, calling it false, while the United States and its Western allies dismissed Russia’s claims as an attempt to create a pretext for escalation.The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) subsequently carried out inspections at three Ukrainian locations identified by Russia and found no indications of undeclared nuclear activities or materials.The immediate casualties from a dirty bomb would largely depend on the conventional explosion rather than radiation exposure, experts say. While radioactive material can cause harm, most such devices would not release enough radiation to kill large numbers of people or cause severe illness across a wide area.However, radioactive dust and smoke can be dangerous, particularly when inhaled close to the blast site. The material could contaminate buildings, public infrastructure and surrounding areas, requiring evacuations and costly clean-up operations.The extent of contamination would depend on the radioactive substance used and how it disperses. In some scenarios, affected buildings and public spaces could remain inaccessible for extended periods.The economic consequences could be substantial even if the immediate health impact was limited. Evacuations, restrictions on access to urban areas and decontamination work could disrupt businesses and public services.The psychological impact is also a major concern. Since radiation cannot be seen, smelled or tasted, people may not know whether they have been exposed. Detecting contamination requires specialised equipment.For this reason, dirty bombs are often described as weapons of terror or mass disruption rather than precision weapons.According to CNN, US intelligence has picked up Iranian communications claiming that bomb-making materials have been stored inside the United States. However, officials remain divided over how credible that information is.Sources familiar with the intelligence told CNN that Iran may not need to bring trained operatives into the country to carry out an attack. It could potentially persuade someone already living in the US to execute a plot.One official said the capability to carry out such an attack had not necessarily increased, but that Iran's incentive to consider one may have changed amid the conflict.US officials are also monitoring separate intelligence suggesting that Iran could use chemical weapons against American troops stationed in the Middle East. The concerns have prompted parallel contingency planning to ensure diplomatic and intelligence personnel in the region have appropriate protective equipment and training.The report also highlighted concerns about the availability of protective equipment and training for US troops in the region.The response to a suspected dirty bomb attack would involve identifying the radioactive material, assessing the extent of contamination and restricting access to affected areas.Specialised equipment would be needed to detect radiation and determine which locations require evacuation or decontamination. Emergency teams would also have to assess the risks to people who may have inhaled or come into contact with radioactive particles.The scale of the response would depend on the type and quantity of material released, the area affected and the level of exposure.As per news agency AP, radioactive contamination could make homes, businesses and public facilities unusable until they had undergone expensive clean-up operations.Depending on the material involved, restrictions could last for months or longer.The primary challenge, therefore, may not necessarily be the number of people killed by radiation but the disruption caused by contamination, evacuation and the difficulty of restoring affected areas to normal use.
Article Summary: US intelligence agencies have detected what officials describe as Iranian planning to potentially target senior members of President Donald Trump's administration in Washington DC. The intelligence has triggered contingency planning in the United States, although officials remain divided over whether Iran has the capability or intention to carry out such an attack. Iran's foreign ministry denied the report and termed the allegations as 'baseless'

Article Title: A Michigan coal plant scheduled to shut down remains open under a seventh federal emergency order despite an appeals court ruling; environmental groups estimate the extensions cost families over $600,
Article Text:
A Michigan coal plant scheduled to shut down remains open under a seventh federal emergency order despite an appeals court ruling; environmental groups estimate the extensions cost families over $600,000 a day/Image: AP

Court ruling challenges federal intervention

Environmental groups raise concerns over costs

Trump administration continues push to support coal industry

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A 64-year-old coal-fired power plant near Grand Rapids, Michigan, will continue operating under a fresh federal emergency order, extending its life beyond the planned retirement date despite a court ruling against the administration's earlier actions.Energy Secretary Chris Wright issued the latest directive late Friday, requiring the J.H. Campbell Generating Plant to remain operational. The department said the facility was needed to protect electricity supplies and reduce the risk of blackouts.The extension is the seventh emergency order issued for the plant since May 2025. Environmental groups have challenged the repeated interventions, estimating that keeping the facility running costs Midwest households more than $600,000 every day, according to AP.The latest order follows a September decision by a three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, which sided with environmental organisations and several states challenging the administration's directives.The court found that the government had not demonstrated an actual emergency under the law to justify keeping the plants operational. The ruling set aside the administration's previous actions as unlawful.The Energy Department has disputed the decision and petitioned for a rehearing before the full appeals court. A decision on whether the case will be reconsidered by the wider bench remains pending, with a possible appeal to the Supreme Court.Michigan, Illinois and Minnesota were among the states that joined environmental groups in challenging the orders.Despite the legal dispute, Wright has maintained that the Campbell facility and other coal-fired plants are necessary to protect electricity reliability. The administration has relied on emergency powers to prevent their scheduled closures.The latest extension has drawn criticism from environmental organisations, which argue that the government has not demonstrated that the Michigan plant is needed to prevent a power shortage or has helped avert an outage.The Sierra Club estimates that keeping the facility operational adds more than $600,000 a day to costs borne by electricity customers across the Midwest.Its Burning Money tracker puts the total cost of federal orders extending the operating lives of fossil fuel plants in six states at more than $600 million. More than half of that amount is attributed to the Campbell plant in Michigan.Jessi Eidbo of the Sierra Club criticised the latest directive, saying: “At a time when prices are soaring and Americans are struggling to make ends meet, the Trump administration’s decision to issue yet another illegal and expensive extension is punishing.”Ted Kelly, director of US clean energy at the Environmental Defense Fund, also questioned the decision.“Instead of saving families’ money and letting the plant retire as planned, the Trump administration keeps putting its thumb on the scale for costly coal,” Kelly said.The extension forms part of President Donald Trump's broader efforts to revive the US coal sector and maintain coal-fired electricity generation.In June, the administration announced plans to spend nearly $700 million supporting coal-fired power plants and coal exports. The Environmental Protection Agency has also repealed regulations limiting greenhouse gas emissions from coal- and gas-powered facilities.The agency, led by Administrator Lee Zeldin, is also seeking to restrict the ability of future administrations to regulate climate pollution from power plants.Wright has defended the use of emergency orders, arguing that keeping certain facilities operational is necessary to maintain a reliable electricity supply. Environmental groups and state governments, however, continue to challenge the legal basis and financial implications of those decisions.The dispute over the Campbell plant remains unresolved as the full appeals court considers whether to take up the case.
Article Summary: The J.H. Campbell Generating Plant near Grand Rapids, Michigan, will continue operating under a fresh federal emergency order. The extension is the seventh emergency order issued for the plant since May 2025. Environmental groups estimate that keeping the facility running costs Midwest households more than $600,000 a day.

Pope Leo on Tuesday said he was not planning to change the Catholic Church's position on allowing married men to become priests, but did not rule out the possibility of a shift in the future. Article Title: A Wisconsin couple wanted to build a backyard fence for their children with special needs, but the HOA refused; years after the $200,000 settlement, they have filed a new lawsuit against 55 neighbours
Article Text:

A dispute over the fence

Not every neighbour was ready to pay

The rest still owe the money

Homeowners Lisa and Michael Newman are back in court, this time against the homeowners association in their De Pere subdivision and dozens of neighbours who never paid their share of an earlier settlement. The couple filed the new suit this autumn, according to NBC 26, nearly two years after their original legal battle over the HOA's refusal to let them build a backyard fence for their five children with special needs. The case now asks whether the association can be held liable for money its members still owe.The Newmans bought their home in the Nazcr Trac subdivision in 2017, before any of their children had been diagnosed with autism. Their first child received a diagnosis shortly after the move, a second followed in 2018, and a third in 2020. Because of their conditions, all three children were "unable to understand dangerous situations or monitor their own safety" and "require extra supervision to prevent them from running away". All three have wandered away from their parents or caregivers on several occasions. The family's request for a backyard fence grew directly out of those safety concerns, according to the court ruling.A fence would let the children play outside without the constant risk of slipping away.The Newmans sued the Nazcr Trac Homeowners Association after it denied permission to build a fence. The couple wanted a backyard fence for their home in De Pere, Wisconsin, because their children have special needs. Following the HOA's refusal, they took the matter to court. That lawsuit ended with the association agreeing to pay the Newmans $200,000. Under the deal, each homeowner in the subdivision was expected to chip in $1,350.The settlement was supposed to end the dispute. However, not every neighbour was enthusiastic about paying their share. Sixty-nine homeowners paid their part after the original lawsuit, but many others did not. Some residents said they had never heard of the fence dispute until the settlement was announced, and they felt the decision had been made without them.One homeowner who received a judgment initially refused to pay. He changed his mind only after getting legal advice. Others stayed quiet, and some are now facing the consequences.Some neighbours described the latest development as a sense of déjà vu. "Why is this coming back to us? It's so unfair," one homeowner, who chose to remain anonymous, told the network.A few others wondered why they had to chip in when they had nothing to do with the dispute. "I did nothing wrong. Why should I pay?" another anonymous homeowner asked.Whether the remaining 55 homeowners have to pay is still a matter of debate, but attorney Victoria Davis Dávila, who represents the Newmans, says they still owe the money. "There's an outstanding judgment. You had the opportunity to pay. You chose not to pay it," attorney Victoria Davis Dávila said.The new lawsuit names the homeowners association along with the homeowners who have not paid. The attorney also warned that if the balance remains unpaid, the association as a whole could be held responsible. That prospect has left people who have already paid feeling stuck in a problem they did not create.One resident who settled his share said the uncertainty had led him to consider moving away from the neighbourhood. He described the situation in a way that many neighbours seemed to share: nobody knows what happens next.Meanwhile, according to the neighbours, the association is looking for legal representation to respond to the new complaint, and its response is due this week. The Newmans want the matter over as much as anyone, their attorney said.For now, though, a fence that was never built still sits at the centre of a neighbourhood that cannot agree on who should pay for it.
Article Summary: Lisa and Michael Newman sued the Nazcr Trac Homeowners Association after it denied permission to build a fence. The couple wanted a backyard fence for their home in De Pere, Wisconsin, because their children have special needs. That lawsuit ended with the association agreeing to pay the Newmans $200,000. Under the deal, each homeowner in the subdivision was expected to chip in $1,350. Not every neighbour was enthusiastic about paying their share.

Case sent back for fresh custody review

A finding of domestic violence does not automatically determine which parent receives primary custody, but courts must explain how such conduct affects children's welfare when making custody decisions. In New York, a mother challenged a Family Court ruling that gave the children's father primary physical placement despite a finding that he had committed domestic violence against her. The dispute reached the state's Appellate Division after she argued that the lower court had failed to properly consider important evidence and the children's best interests.In a November 13, 2026, decision in Matter of Castro v. Hawkins, available on Justia, the New York Supreme Court's Appellate Division, Fourth Department, reversed the lower court's order and sent the case back for further proceedings. The appeals judges found that the Family Court had not adequately explained its factual findings, assessed the parents' credibility or explained how the finding of domestic violence factored into its custody decision. However, the appellate ruling did not immediately change where the children would live. The existing custody and visitation arrangements will remain in effect until the Family Court makes a fresh determination.The case involved Edward Castro, the father, and Ashley Hawkins, the mother, who were involved in a custody proceeding under New York's Family Court Act. Castro had petitioned the Family Court in Steuben County to modify an earlier custody order. Following the proceedings, the court issued an order on August 6, 2025, granting the parents joint legal custody while awarding the father primary physical placement of their children.Hawkins challenged that decision, arguing that the court had not properly evaluated the circumstances before changing the existing custody arrangement. The appeals court noted that the Family Court had failed to make specific credibility determinations or factual findings on disputed matters raised during the custody hearing. Such findings are important because the trial court is in a better position to assess witnesses and determine whether their accounts are reliable.The judges also explained that an established custody arrangement should only be changed when there is a change in circumstances demonstrating a real need for modification in the children's best interests. However, the lower court had not expressly determined whether the father had established the required change in circumstances before considering whether awarding him primary placement would benefit the children.One of the significant issues involved the Family Court's finding that the father had committed an act of domestic violence against the mother. The appeals judges said that once such a finding had been made, the lower court was required to consider how the domestic violence affected the children's best interests, alongside other relevant circumstances. It also had to explain on the record how that finding influenced its custody decision. The Family Court had not provided the required explanation.Hawkins also argued that the court had improperly penalised her for reporting suspected child abuse under New York's Social Services Law. However, the appeals court said the available record was insufficient to determine whether this had happened because the lower court had not expressly decided whether her reports were false or made in bad faith.The judges also identified another problem with the original decision. The Family Court had relied on information that was not established during the proceedings, including the number of child abuse reports the mother had made against the father during the previous year and an alleged complaint she had filed against him with the FBI. The appeals court said that relying on facts outside the record was an error because judicial decisions must be based on the evidence presented at the hearing.The Appellate Division also found that the Family Court had not sufficiently examined several factors relevant to determining the children's best interests. These include each parent's ability to provide a suitable home, their emotional and financial capacity to care for the children, the stability of previous living arrangements, the children's relationships with their siblings and, where relevant, their own preferences. Because the lower court had not properly evaluated these issues, the appeals judges said they could not independently determine which custody arrangement would best serve the children.On November 13, 2026, the Fourth Department unanimously reversed the August 2025 order on legal grounds and returned the matter to Steuben County Family Court. The lower court must now make specific findings about whether the father had established the required change in circumstances and whether modifying the previous custody arrangement is in the children's best interests.It may hold an additional hearing if necessary.Importantly, the appeals court directed that the existing custody and visitation provisions remain effective while the case is reconsidered. This means the father retains primary physical placement for now, and the mother has not yet secured a change in custody. The decision therefore requires a more complete judicial review rather than an immediate transfer of the children to either parent.

Article Title: Reba McEntire opened her personal archive for a 255-lot Nashville charity auction in October, offering five decades of stage gowns, jewellery and keepsakes to support the Reba McEntire Fund and its no
Article Text:

A dress worn on a country music awards stage, a rhinestone-covered suit from a television singing competition and scripts marked with handwritten notes from a sitcom career spanning six years, these were among the personal keepsakes Reba McEntire put up for auction as she opened a window into five decades of her life in entertainment. The country music star's collection went under the hammer in Nashville on October 23, with 255 lots offered through Julien’s Auctions to benefit the Reba McEntire Fund and its nonprofit initiatives across the US.Titled 'The Reba Collection', the benefit auction was held at the Musicians Hall of Fame & Museum at the Historic Nashville Municipal Auditorium. The collection brought together pieces from McEntire's wardrobe, jewellery box and professional archive, including stage and screen-worn gowns, boots, belt buckles, awards, jewellery and personal memorabilia. According to the auction announcement on McEntire's official website, all proceeds were designated to support the fund.For McEntire, the sale was an opportunity to let fans take home something more personal than conventional merchandise. The singer said her team had carefully looked after the clothes over the years, but she felt it was time for them to move on and find new homes. She added that buyers would have both the outfit and the story behind it, knowing that she had worn the piece herself.The collection offered a timeline of a career that moved between country music stages, television studios and film sets. McEntire, who has sold more than 58 million albums worldwide and recorded 35 career No. 1 singles, has spent more than five decades building a presence across entertainment. A member of the Country Music Hall of Fame and a recipient of the 2018 Kennedy Center Honors, she has also starred in her own sitcom and appeared as a coach on NBC's 'The Voice'.Some of the most recognisable pieces in the auction came from her appearances at major country music events. Among them was a forest-green silk gown with leather-studded trim that McEntire wore at the 2009 Academy of Country Music Awards in Las Vegas. The ceremony was significant for another reason: it marked her 11th time hosting the awards. The gown was offered with a signed photograph. Another highlight was a silver tinsel Roberto Cavalli dress and matching heels worn at the 1987 Academy of Country Music Awards and later for Bob Hope's television Christmas special. The outfit reflected the theatrical side of McEntire's stage image, which became known for its elaborate silhouettes, embellishments and frequent changes during performances.The catalogue also reached into her television career. Three personal final-draft scripts from her sitcom 'Reba', which ran from 2001 to 2007, were included in the sale. The scripts were signed and carried handwritten annotations throughout, offering a glimpse of the preparation behind the show. One was labelled as her study script for a Tuesday recording, with changes noted up to 1.50 pm. Two scripts from NBC's 'Happy's Place', which premiered in 2024, were also part of the collection.Her more recent television appearances were represented by a rhinestone-covered hot-pink suit worn on 'The Voice' in 2023. Other items included her signature boots and belt buckles, awards and a Franck Muller 18-karat rose-gold watch set with diamonds. The auction catalogue also featured a personalised bronze belt buckle bearing her name, accompanied by its original signed box.For fans, the appeal lay in the opportunity to own an object connected to a particular moment in her career. For the singer, the sale also meant that items carefully preserved by her team could continue to be appreciated rather than remain in storage. The charitable beneficiary was central to the event. The Reba McEntire Fund was created by the singer to support projects across the United States. Its stated priorities include improving the health and well-being of families, recognising and supporting those who have served, and creating opportunities for young people.The auction announcement said the sale was intended to generate both financial support and awareness for local and national nonprofit initiatives.The fund's three areas of focus reflect causes that extend beyond the music industry. Family well-being, support for veterans and opportunities for young people are the broad themes through which it backs charitable work. By directing the auction proceeds towards the fund, McEntire connected objects from her own professional journey with initiatives intended to benefit communities.Julien’s Auctions co-founder and executive director Martin Nolan said the collection offered fans a personal connection to the memories and milestones that shaped McEntire's career. The auction house described the sale as a celebration of five decades of fashion and entertainment, bringing together material from her work in music, television and film.
Article Summary: Country music star's collection went under the hammer in Nashville on October 23. 255 lots were offered through Julien’s Auctions to benefit the Reba McEntire Fund and its nonprofit initiatives across the US.
